geo.title: SSS Proved from SAS
geo.target:
I can follow and explain a proof of SSS using SAS and isosceles triangles, covering every case of where the joining segment falls.
Two-day lesson: Day 1 interior case; Day 2 exterior and endpoint cases.

slides.title: Day 1: get started
slides.html:
Rigid frames: a triangle of straws stays rigid but a square frame wobbles. Why? Students push on both.

  • I can explain the plan of the SSS proof: build a SAS copy on the other side of AB from the Ruler and Protractor Postulates, then use isosceles triangles.
  • I can finish all three cases (interior, exterior, endpoint) and say why SSS is a theorem in this course and why its proof may not use SSS.

geo.body:
Rigid frames: a triangle of straws stays rigid but a square frame wobbles. Why? Students push on both.

  • I can explain the plan of the SSS proof: build a SAS copy on the other side of AB from the Ruler and Protractor Postulates, then use isosceles triangles.
  • I can finish all three cases (interior, exterior, endpoint) and say why SSS is a theorem in this course and why its proof may not use SSS.

slides.title: Day 1: the big idea
slides.html: SSS is proved from SAS and the isosceles theorems. In this course it is a theorem, not a postulate.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Day 1. Proof of SSS, interior case (adapted from Theorem 11, Jacobs p. 164).

Read the worked steps
StepReason
AB = DE, AC = DF and BC = EF.The original givens. Goal: triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF.
On the side of line AB away from C, draw ray AG so that angle BAG = angle EDF.Angle existence and uniqueness (Protractor Postulate). This is not the compass angle copy from 4.12, which needs SSS. The angle is between 0 and 180 degrees because DEF is a real triangle.
On that ray, choose G so that AG = DF.Segment existence and uniqueness (Ruler Postulate). DF is more than 0, so G exists, is not A, and is off line AB.
Triangle ABG ≅ triangle DEF, so BG = EF.SAS (AB = DE, AG = DF, included angle BAG = EDF), then CPCTC.
AC = AG and BC = BG.AC = DF and AG = DF; BC = EF and BG = EF.
Draw CG. In this case, CG crosses AB between A and B.The interior case, taught on Day 1.
Triangles ACG and BCG are isosceles, so angle ACG = angle AGC and angle BCG = angle BGC.Theorem 9.
Add: angle ACB = angle ACG + angle BCG = angle AGC + angle BGC = angle AGB.Angle addition, because CG runs inside both angles.
Triangle ABC ≅ triangle ABG.SAS: AC = AG, included angle ACB = AGB, BC = BG.
Triangle ABG ≅ triangle DEF, so triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF.Two triangles congruent to the same triangle are congruent to each other. A matches D, B matches E, G matches F.

geo.title: Worked example
geo.prompt: Day 1. Proof of SSS, interior case (adapted from Theorem 11, Jacobs p. 164).

steps.step: AB = DE, AC = DF and BC = EF.
steps.reason: The original givens. Goal: triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF.

steps.step: On the side of line AB away from C, draw ray AG so that angle BAG = angle EDF.
steps.reason: Angle existence and uniqueness (Protractor Postulate). This is not the compass angle copy from 4.12, which needs SSS. The angle is between 0 and 180 degrees because DEF is a real triangle.

steps.step: On that ray, choose G so that AG = DF.
steps.reason: Segment existence and uniqueness (Ruler Postulate). DF is more than 0, so G exists, is not A, and is off line AB.

steps.step: Triangle ABG ≅ triangle DEF, so BG = EF.
steps.reason: SAS (AB = DE, AG = DF, included angle BAG = EDF), then CPCTC.
AC = DF and AG = DF; BC = EF and BG = EF.

steps.step: Draw CG. In this case, CG crosses AB between A and B.
steps.reason: The interior case, taught on Day 1.

steps.step: Triangles ACG and BCG are isosceles, so angle ACG = angle AGC and angle BCG = angle BGC.
Add: angle ACB = angle ACG + angle BCG = angle AGC + angle BGC = angle AGB.
steps.reason: Angle addition, because CG runs inside both angles.
SAS: AC = AG, included angle ACB = AGB, BC = BG.

steps.step: Triangle ABG ≅ triangle DEF, so triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF.
steps.reason: Two triangles congruent to the same triangle are congruent to each other. A matches D, B matches E, G matches F.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Day 2. The exterior and endpoint cases (same setup as Day 1, rows 1 to 5).

Read the worked steps
StepReason
The line CG can cross outside the segment past A or past B. It can also pass right through A or through B. We only need to prove the past-B and through-B cases. The A cases work the same way: swap the names A and B, and swap D and E in the other triangle.Swapping A with B and D with E turns the givens AC=DF and BC=EF into each other, so we have exactly the same facts, and every matching side and SAS step still works.
Exterior case: line CG meets line AB outside segment AB, past B.Same G, same equal sides as Day 1.
Here angle ACG is the larger angle at C and angle BCG is the smaller one. At G, angle AGC is larger and angle BGC is smaller.Name the angles before subtracting.
Angle ACG = angle AGC and angle BCG = angle BGC.Theorem 9 in triangles ACG and BCG.
Subtract: angle ACB = angle ACG - angle BCG = angle AGC - angle BGC = angle AGB.Angle subtraction.
Endpoint case: CG passes through B, so C, B and G are on one line.The endpoint representative after that relabeling.
Then ray CB is ray CG and ray GB is ray GC, so angle ACB is angle ACG and angle AGB is angle AGC.The rays along CG are the rays through B.
Triangle ACG is isosceles (AC = AG), so angle ACG = angle AGC. That means angle ACB = angle AGB.Theorem 9 in the one triangle that remains.
In every case, SAS gives triangle ABC ≅ triangle ABG, and the Day 1 finish gives triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF.So SSS holds for all triangles before 4.12 to 4.14 use it.

geo.title: Worked example
geo.prompt: Day 2. The exterior and endpoint cases (same setup as Day 1, rows 1 to 5).

steps.step: The line CG can cross outside the segment past A or past B. It can also pass right through A or through B. We only need to prove the past-B and through-B cases. The A cases work the same way: swap the names A and B, and swap D and E in the other triangle.
steps.reason: Swapping A with B and D with E turns the givens AC=DF and BC=EF into each other, so we have exactly the same facts, and every matching side and SAS step still works.

steps.step: Exterior case: line CG meets line AB outside segment AB, past B.
steps.reason: Same G, same equal sides as Day 1.

steps.step: Here angle ACG is the larger angle at C and angle BCG is the smaller one. At G, angle AGC is larger and angle BGC is smaller.
Angle ACG = angle AGC and angle BCG = angle BGC.
steps.reason: Theorem 9 in triangles ACG and BCG.

steps.step: Subtract: angle ACB = angle ACG - angle BCG = angle AGC - angle BGC = angle AGB.
Endpoint case: CG passes through B, so C, B and G are on one line.
steps.reason: The endpoint representative after that relabeling.

steps.step: Then ray CB is ray CG and ray GB is ray GC, so angle ACB is angle ACG and angle AGB is angle AGC.
steps.reason: The rays along CG are the rays through B.

steps.step: Triangle ACG is isosceles (AC = AG), so angle ACG = angle AGC. That means angle ACB = angle AGB.
steps.reason: Theorem 9 in the one triangle that remains.

steps.step: In every case, SAS gives triangle ABC ≅ triangle ABG, and the Day 1 finish gives triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF.
steps.reason: So SSS holds for all triangles before 4.12 to 4.14 use it.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Jordan says SSS is a postulate in this course.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

'SSS is a postulate in this course' is the misconception. SSS is a theorem proved from SAS here. (Some other valid axiom systems do postulate SSS.) A complete proof covers all three cases, which is why Day 2 exists.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
Two triangles both have sides 3, 4 and 5. Are they congruent?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Yes, by SSS.

Reveal second check

A flip may change which way it faces, but not the lengths.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Can the SSS proof use SSS for its helper triangles?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. It uses the isosceles base-angle theorem, which came from SAS.

Reveal second check

Nothing in the proof leans on SSS itself.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html:
Why is a triangle frame rigid but a square frame wobbly?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

SSS: three fixed sides fix the triangle's angles. Four fixed sides do not fix a quadrilateral's angles.

Reveal second check

Name the givens and the theorem or definition used.
